title: Of experience
hook: the book's last essay: know yourself through ordinary life (Essays 3.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, haven't you lived? Montaigne's answer to I've done nothing today. Your line was haven't I lived. Which three moments made your list last night? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

Some kitchens have a cook who never measures. A pinch of this, a splash of that, and somehow it comes out right. Ask for the recipe and the answer is a shrug: you just get a feel for it. Nobody taught that cook in a classroom. Ordinary dinners did, one after another. Montaigne ends his whole book with an essay built on that kind of knowing. It's called Of experience, and it asks where we really learn who we are. His answer is not in the library. It's in the kitchen, the sickbed, the bad temper, the night's sleep.
screen: `THE COOK WHO NEVER MEASURES.` → `A THOUSAND ORDINARY DINNERS.` → `THE LAST ESSAY: OF EXPERIENCE.`

segments.voice: First, where the essay starts. Montaigne says the desire to know is natural to us, and we try every road to it. When reason isn't enough, we turn to experience. Then he spends pages showing how slippery reason gets. Laws pile up and still can't fit every case, because life keeps producing new ones. Second, his turn inward. He says he studies himself more than any other subject. That, he says, is his metaphysics and his physics. It isn't a boast. He's simply the one case he can watch up close, every day. Third, what he actually learns. If someone remembers how far their last anger carried them, he says, they'll see its ugliness better than in any book of philosophy. The same goes, he says, for errors of judgment: remember how often you were sure and wrong, and you'll trust the next certainty less. His teachers are his own illnesses, his own moods, his own mistakes, looked at honestly. Fourth, where it ends. Montaigne says the finest lives are the ones that fit the ordinary human pattern, without miracles and without extravagance. And he closes the book not with a grand theory but with a wish for a healthy old age, borrowed from the Roman poet Horace. That's the shape of the essay: from the hunger to know everything, down to the plain lesson of one ordinary life. The cook's way of knowing, turned on the self.
screen: `WHEN REASON FAILS, EXPERIENCE.` · `I STUDY MYSELF.` · `REMEMBER YOUR LAST ANGER.` · `THE ORDINARY HUMAN PATTERN.` · then, large: `ORDINARY LESSONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one ordinary lesson. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring back one small, recent moment that went a little wrong. A snapped answer. A late night that cost you the morning. A meal that sat badly. Don't scold yourself. Just look at it the way Montaigne looked at his own fits of temper, like a fair witness. What did it actually teach? Let the lesson be small and plain. Hold it. The bell holds the time.
Of experience. The last essay of Montaigne's book, where he says he studies himself more than anything, and learns most from the plain lessons of his own ordinary life. Today's word.
Your line: ordinary lessons. Before bed, write down one thing today taught you that no book did. One sentence is plenty. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Readers often treat Of experience as the place where Montaigne's book gathers itself: he turns from theories and laws to what his own body, moods and mistakes have taught him.

what it means: for Montaigne, it's the plain lessons of one ordinary life, studied honestly from the inside.
what a scholar hears: the last essay moves from the limits of reason and law to self-study, and closes the whole book with lines from Horace asking for a sound and healthy old age.

notes: Confirm the essay closes with lines from Horace, Odes 1.31, asking Apollo for a healthy old age with a sound mind; the script says only 'a wish for a healthy old age, borrowed from the Roman poet Horace' and does not name Apollo.
'The finest lives' paraphrases Montaigne's own superlative ('les plus belles vies'); confirm.
'Not because he's the most interesting man alive' is the narrator's aside, not a claim about Montaigne; cut if it reads as a superlative.
The kitchen-cook hook is an illustration, not a source claim.
